science-source-y7-b10-d12.title: Year 7 Science — Forces — Aranmore (original assessment)
science-source-y7-b10-d12.coverage: Original source MC, with original graph/table where required. Ambiguous questions retained manually in the bank, not automatic battles.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a force?
questions.explanation: D. Pushes, pulls and twists are all examples of forces.

questions.prompt: In what units is force measured?
questions.explanation: B. Force is measured in newtons (N).

questions.prompt: A pulling force can be measured by using a?
questions.explanation: C. A spring balance can measure a pulling force.

questions.prompt: An example of an unbalanced force is?
options: Caleb sitting quietly on a chair.
Jacob travelling on his bike at a constant speed.
Michelle lying down looking at the sky.
Mr Norgrove speeding up in his car.
questions.explanation: D. Speeding up requires a nonzero resultant force; constant speed would also need a straight path to imply zero acceleration.

questions.prompt: The physics law of Inertia can be described as?
options: An object will change its shape when it is moved.
An object will want to keep doing what is already doing.
A theory that no one fully understands.
Driving really fast in a car.
questions.explanation: B is the informal intended answer: inertia is resistance to change in velocity; objects do not literally “want” to do anything.

questions.prompt: The effect of mass on inertia is?
options: The larger the mass the smaller the inertia.
The smaller the inertia the larger the mass.
The larger the mass the larger the inertia..
questions.explanation: C. Greater mass means greater inertia.

questions.prompt: An example of something that protects from inertia while in a car is?
questions.explanation: D. Seatbelts and airbags exert forces to change occupant momentum more safely over a longer time.

questions.prompt: The force that slows objects down is called?
questions.explanation: C. Friction opposes relative sliding or its tendency; it does not always oppose the overall motion of an object.

questions.prompt: The amount of friction depends on?
options: How hard the surfaces are pushed together.
The heat stored in the object.
questions.explanation: D. In the elementary dry-friction model, surface interaction and normal force affect friction.

questions.prompt: An example of unwanted friction would be:
options: your shoe gripping the ground while walking.
a cars brakes slowing it down.
the rubbing of the engine pistons inside a car.
questions.explanation: D. Friction between engine parts dissipates energy and causes wear.

questions.prompt: A method of reducing friction could be:
options: pushing instead of pulling an object.
increasing the surface area of both objects.
questions.explanation: A. Suitable lubrication can reduce friction between surfaces.

questions.prompt: A non-contact force can be described as:
options: a force that changes objects without us knowing.
the strongest force in the universe.
a force that moves objects without direct contact.
a force that moves objects by direct contact.
questions.explanation: C. A non-contact force acts without surfaces touching (and need not cause motion if balanced).

questions.prompt: An example of a non-contact force could be:
options: an ice skate sliding on ice.
a man falling from a plane.
a person twisting open a jar of peanut butter.
questions.explanation: C. Gravity acts on the falling person without contact with Earth; air resistance also acts.

questions.prompt: The three elements that are magnetic are?
questions.explanation: C. Iron, nickel and cobalt are familiar ferromagnetic elements under ordinary conditions.

science-source-y8-b10-d13.title: Year 8 Science — Cells and body systems (original assessment)
science-source-y8-b10-d13.coverage: Original source MC, with original graph/table where required. Ambiguous questions retained manually in the bank, not automatic battles.

questions.prompt: A specimen prepared for a normal classroom light microscope needs to be very thin so;
options: the cover slip sits nicely on top of it.
it fits in the field of view.
questions.explanation: B. Light must pass through a thin specimen in a normal transmitted-light classroom microscope.

questions.prompt: A micrometre is:
questions.explanation: A. 1 micrometre = 0.001 mm.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true:
options: only plant cells have a cell membrane.
both plant and animal cells contain a nucleus.
questions.explanation: D in the general school model: typical plant and animal cells both have nuclei; exceptions include mature mammalian red blood cells and some specialised plant cells.

questions.prompt: Nerve cells:
options: carry information from your brain to other parts of your body.
come in three types, voluntary, involuntary and cardiac.
produce heat for the body and store energy.
questions.explanation: A. Nerve cells transmit information through the nervous system.

questions.prompt: The four types of tissue in the human body are:
questions.explanation: D. The four principal tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue.

questions.prompt: Stem cells are:
options: cells that are found in plant stems.
cells that have a special job to do.
cells that become different types of cells under specific conditions.
cells that work in pairs to open and close the stomata.
questions.explanation: C. Stem cells can differentiate into specialised cell types under appropriate conditions.

questions.prompt: Gas exchange in the lungs occurs at the:
questions.explanation: B. Alveoli are the main gas-exchange structures.

questions.prompt: Food in the stomach undergoes:
questions.explanation: A. The stomach churns food and performs chemical digestion.

science-source-y10-b10-d24.title: Year 10 Science — Chemistry — Aranmore 2011 (original assessment)
science-source-y10-b10-d24.coverage: Original source MC, with original graph/table where required. Ambiguous questions retained manually in the bank, not automatic battles.

questions.prompt: Which of the following elements has 6 protons in its nucleus?
questions.explanation: C. Carbon has atomic number 6, hence 6 protons.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are all transition metals?
questions.explanation: B. Manganese, iron and copper are transition metals.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are all alkali metals?
questions.explanation: A. Lithium, sodium and potassium are group-1 alkali metals.

questions.prompt: A covalent bond is...
options: A bond between two or more different metals.
A bond between two or more non metals.
A secret name for James Bond.
questions.explanation: C is the best school-level description: covalent bonds involve shared electron pairs, commonly between nonmetal atoms.

questions.prompt: Which of the following all have 2 valence electrons?
questions.explanation: D. Beryllium, calcium and magnesium are group-2 elements with two outer-shell electrons in their neutral atoms.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are noble gases?
questions.explanation: A. Neon, argon and helium are noble gases.

questions.prompt: Which of the following ionic formulae are ALL correct?
questions.explanation: B. MgO, MgCl₂ and Mg₃(PO₄)₂ all balance the usual ionic charges.

questions.prompt: The valence electrons are:
options: the number of total electrons an atom has.
the number of electrons in the atom's outer shell.
the number of electrons an atom has after it reacts.
the number of electrons an atom has before it reacts.
questions.explanation: B. Valence electrons occupy the outer shell in this elementary model.

questions.prompt: What are the elements in group one (1) of the periodic table called?
questions.explanation: B. Group-1 metals are alkali metals (hydrogen is an exception to calling all group members metals).

questions.prompt: The mass number of an element is how many ____________ there are one atom.
questions.explanation: D. Mass number is protons plus neutrons in a specified isotope, not a universal fixed number for an element.

science-source-y10-b10-d27.title: Year 10 Science — Chemistry extension — Safety Bay 2017 (original assessment)
science-source-y10-b10-d27.coverage: Original source MC, with original graph/table where required. Ambiguous questions retained manually in the bank, not automatic battles.

questions.prompt: Which of the following particles are used in determining the position of an element within the periodic table?
questions.explanation: A. Element order is defined by proton number (atomic number); electron configuration explains much of the periodic pattern.

questions.prompt: Sodium has 11 electrons. When it is in its ground state, its electron configuration is:
questions.explanation: B. Neutral sodium ground-state shell configuration is2:8:1.

questions.prompt: An atom has an electron configuration of 2:8:8:1. What group would it be in?
questions.explanation: A. One outer electron in2:8:8:1 indicates group1.

questions.prompt: Covalent bonds occur between
options: non - metal atoms and other non -  metal atoms.
questions.explanation: C. Covalent bonding commonly occurs between nonmetal atoms and involves shared electrons.

questions.prompt: Carbon has an electron configuration of 2:4 and is in group 14. Carbon bonds covalently with hydrogen to form a molecule called methane. Which is the most likely formula for this molecule?
questions.explanation: A. Carbon commonly forms four covalent bonds: CH₄.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not true regarding noble gases?
options: They are known as inert gases.
All their atoms have 8 electrons in their outer shell.
They are very stable, tending NOT to bond or react with other atoms.
questions.explanation: C is false: helium has a full first shell with2 electrons, not8. Noble gases are relatively unreactive, but some can form compounds.

questions.prompt: Nitrogen is in period 2, group15. Which of the following elements would have properties most similar to nitrogen?
questions.explanation: A. Phosphorus is in the same group15 as nitrogen.

questions.prompt: Haematite, Fe2O3, is not found in the periodic table because
options: it has properties different from the metals in any other group.
it is only a recent discovery.
its relative atomic mass is too great.
questions.explanation: B. Fe₂O₃ is a compound, not an element.

questions.prompt: Bonds that form between a metal and a non-metal are called:
questions.explanation: B. The elementary metal/nonmetal model describes ionic bonding: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

questions.prompt: The Law of Conservation of Mass states that during a chemical reaction atoms cannot be created or destroyed. From this Law, it follows that during a chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants and products:
questions.explanation: D. In a closed system, total mass is conserved during ordinary chemical reactions.

questions.prompt:
The chemical reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid can be represented by the following equation: CaCO3 + 2HC1 CaCl2 + CO2 + H20 The carbon dioxide gas (CO2) produced by this reaction can be collected and its volume measured. The following graph represents the volume of carbon dioxide produced over a time period from 0 to 270 seconds when some solid calcium carbonate is reacted with an excess amount of hydrochloric acid. After how many seconds, from the start of the reaction, had half of the original amount of calcium carbonate reacted?
[LV-MEDIA:{"images":[{"pack":"repo-science-batch10","id":"reaction-graph"}]}]
questions.explanation: A. The plateau is about40 mL, so half reaction corresponds to20 mL, reached at about60 seconds.

questions.prompt: The term solubility is used to describe how well a compound dissolves. Scientists use a solubility table like the one below to determine how soluble or insoluble a compound will be in water. Using this table, determine which of the following compounds is insoluble. Source table: nitrates soluble; chlorides/bromides/iodides soluble except silver, mercury and lead; sulfates soluble except calcium, barium, lead and silver; carbonates/phosphates generally insoluble except alkali-metal and ammonium salts.
questions.explanation: D. PbSO₄ is listed as a sulfate exception and treated as insoluble in the supplied table. The table contains NH₃⁺/charge typos; ammonium isNH₄⁺.
